body:
The main gotcha with linking to an external `importmap.json` is that `importmap.json` needs to be fetched and parsed before *any* specifier resolution can happen. This was mentioned in [this CRBug comment](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40609602#comment2), but I can't find the spec discussions referenced there. 

This is also a concern with `<link rel=importmap href="importmap.json">`, and at that point the parser has already started. Would it need to postpone script execution until `importmap.json` is fetched and parsed (so that specifier resolution can work based on `importmap.json`)?

This isn't the case with inline import maps because there's no fetch involved. @yoavweiss might have some more context on this situation that I'm missing.

> * No ordering effects of the flavor "whoops, my module loaded before my import map, what to do?". Nothing is available sooner!

I don't believe this is correct. As @KurtCattiSchmidt points out, the availability of the header doesn't mean that the map is available, just discovered. The browser would still need to fetch it.

While multiple import maps enable to do that without blocking scripts (or failing), this will still be racy.

I'm also not sure that we'd want any passive resource (e.g. images) to be able to define import maps, as that could have meaningful implications.

@yoavweiss 
> > * No ordering effects of the flavor "whoops, my module loaded before my import map, what to do?". Nothing is available sooner!
> 
> I don't believe this is correct. As [@KurtCattiSchmidt](https://github.com/KurtCattiSchmidt) points out, the availability of the header doesn't mean that the map is available, just discovered. The browser would still need to fetch it.
>
> While multiple import maps enable to do that without blocking scripts (or failing), this will still be racy.

I was assuming it would work like a blocking script, but agree that’s suboptimal.

How feasible would something like this be:

- Maintain a set _I_ of all import maps currently in progress (loading, parsing, etc)
- Once an import map is either completely processed OR fails to load, remove from the set
- Then, in specifier resolution:
	- If the specifier can already be resolved → no change
	- If the specifier cannot be resolved → wait until I is empty and then try again (or even after every change). This would not be observable, the semantics would be as if the URL took a longer time to resolve.

> I'm also not sure that we'd want any passive resource (e.g. images) to be able to define import maps, as that could have meaningful implications.

I should have clarified: Import maps defined by resources should absolutely not leak outside the scope of that resource and its subresources (and their subresources and so on). For example:
- For an HTML page: all resources in the document
- For a CSS file: that CSS file and any resources it imports
- For a JS file: that JS file, its imports, any workers it spawns, any of its fetches, etc

(This is obviously extremely handwavy, but you get the idea.)

Therefore, for an image, this would not really be meaningful, since it does not load any subresources (except SVG, which also doesn't load subresources when used as an image).

> How feasible would something like this be:
> 
> * Maintain a set _I_ of all import maps currently in progress (loading, parsing, etc)
> * Once an import map is either completely processed OR fails to load, remove from the set
> * Then, in specifier resolution:
>   
>   * If the specifier can already be resolved → no change
>   * If the specifier cannot be resolved → wait until I is empty and then try again (or even after every change). This would not be observable, the semantics would be as if the URL took a longer time to resolve.

That sounds feasible, but a bit complex and still a potential source of slowness. It'd be good to think of the use cases in terms of:
* How often would that block assets from loading, and for how long?
* How would developers optimize that away?



> * For an HTML page: all resources in the document
> * For a CSS file: that CSS file and any resources it imports
> * For a JS file: that JS file, its imports, any workers it spawns, any of its fetches, etc

That would be a significant change from the current import map model, where there's one global one for the document. (even when there are multiple import maps, they get merged into the document's [global object's map](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-global-import-map))

This feels it would require something like [Task Attribution](https://wicg.github.io/soft-navigations/#sec-task-attribution-algorithms) to properly account for e.g. modules injected by scripts in Tasks or MicroTasks they spin off.

> > How feasible would something like this be:
> > 
> > * Maintain a set _I_ of all import maps currently in progress (loading, parsing, etc)
> > * Once an import map is either completely processed OR fails to load, remove from the set
> > * Then, in specifier resolution:
> >   
> >   * If the specifier can already be resolved → no change
> >   * If the specifier cannot be resolved → wait until I is empty and then try again (or even after every change). This would not be observable, the semantics would be as if the URL took a longer time to resolve.
> 
> That sounds feasible, but a bit complex and still a potential source of slowness. It'd be good to think of the use cases in terms of:
> 
> * How often would that block assets from loading, and for how long?

Import map management tools (e.g. JSPM) have already started using injector scripts, and this could be designed to be no slower.

> * How would developers optimize that away?

Inline either the whole map, or a part of it. This does not *remove* inline import maps. It just makes them a perf optimization instead of the only way.

> > * For an HTML page: all resources in the document
> > * For a CSS file: that CSS file and any resources it imports
> > * For a JS file: that JS file, its imports, any workers it spawns, any of its fetches, etc
> 
> That would be a significant change from the current import map model, where there's one global one for the document. (even when there are multiple import maps, they get merged into the document's [global object's map](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-global-import-map))

I was assuming they'd be merged into `scopes`.
Isn't this exactly how scopes work? (with some extrapolation on "[referring script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#the-resolution-algorithm)"…)

> I was assuming they'd be merged into `scopes`.

That would work better with the current model.



> Isn't this exactly how scopes work? (with some extrapolation on "[referring script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#the-resolution-algorithm)"…)

Yeah, good point. I'm adding a [WPT](https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/7622812) to make sure that actually works today..
